'''Adiabatic quantum computation''' ('''AQC''') is a form of [[quantum computing]] which relies on the [[adiabatic theorem]] to perform calculations<ref name="Farhi2000">{{cite arXiv |last1=Farhi |first1=E. |last2=Goldstone |first2=Jeffrey |author-link2=Jeffrey Goldstone |last3=Gutmann |first3=S. |last4=Sipser |first4=M. |author-link4=Michael Sipser |eprint=quant-ph/0001106v1 |title=Quantum Computation by Adiabatic Evolution |year=2000 }}</ref> and is closely related to [[quantum annealing]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kadowaki |first1=T. |last2=Nishimori |first2=H. |title=Quantum annealing in the transverse Ising model |journal=Physical Review E |volume=58 |issue=5 |page=5355 |date=1998-11-01 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.58.5355|arxiv = cond-mat/9804280 |bibcode = 1998PhRvE..58.5355K |s2cid=36114913 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Finilla |first1=A. B. |last2=Gomez |first2=M. A. |last3=Sebenik |first3=C. |last4=Doll |first4=D. J. |date=1994-03-18 |title=Quantum annealing: A new method for minimizing multidimensional functions |journal=Chemical Physics Letters |volume=219 |issue=5 |pages=343–348 |arxiv=chem-ph/9404003 |bibcode=1994CPL...219..343F |doi=10.1016/0009-2614(94)00117-0 |s2cid=97302385}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Santoro |first1=G. E. |last2=Tosatti |first2=E. |date=2006-09-08 |title=Optimization using quantum mechanics: quantum annealing through adiabatic evolution |journal=Journal of Physics A |volume=39 |issue=36 |page=R393 |bibcode=2006JPhA...39R.393S |doi=10.1088/0305-4470/39/36/R01 |s2cid=116931586}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Das |first1=A. |last2=Chakrabarti |first2=B. K. |date=2008-09-05 |title=Colloquium: Quantum annealing and analog quantum computation |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=80 |issue=3 |page=1061 |arxiv=0801.2193 |bibcode=2008RvMP...80.1061D |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.80.1061 |s2cid=14255125}}</ref>

==Description==
First, a (potentially complicated) [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] is found whose ground state describes the solution to the problem of interest. Next, a system with a simple [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] is prepared and initialized to the ground state. Finally, the simple Hamiltonian is adiabatically evolved to the desired complicated Hamiltonian. By the adiabatic theorem, the system remains in the ground state, so at the end, the state of the system describes the solution to the problem. Adiabatic quantum computing has been shown to be polynomially equivalent to conventional quantum computing in the circuit model.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Aharonov |first1=Dorit |author-link1=Dorit Aharonov |last2=van Dam |first2=Wim |last3=Kempe |first3=Julia | author3-link = Julia Kempe |last4=Landau |first4=Zeph |last5=LLoyd |first5=Seth |title=Adiabatic Quantum Computation is Equivalent to Standard Quantum Computation |journal=SIAM Journal on Computing |volume=37 |page=166 |date=2007-04-01 |doi=10.1137/s0097539705447323|arxiv=quant-ph/0405098 }}</ref>

The time complexity for an adiabatic algorithm is the time taken to complete the adiabatic evolution which is dependent on the gap in the energy [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]] ([[Spectral gap (physics)|spectral gap]]) of the Hamiltonian. Specifically, if the system is to be kept in the ground state, the energy gap between the ground state and the first excited state of <math>H(t)</math> provides an upper bound on the rate at which the Hamiltonian can be evolved at time {{nowrap|<math>t</math>.}}<ref>{{cite journal |last1=van Dam |first1=Wim |last2=van Mosca |first2=Michele |last3=Vazirani |first3=Umesh |title=How Powerful is Adiabatic Quantum Computation? |journal=Proceedings of the 42nd Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science |page=279}}</ref> When the spectral gap is small, the Hamiltonian has to be evolved slowly. The runtime for the entire algorithm can be bounded by:

<math>T = O\left(\frac{1}{g_{min}^2}\right)</math>

where <math>g_{min}</math> is the minimum spectral gap for {{nowrap|<math>H(t)</math>.}}

AQC is a possible method to get around the problem of [[Quantum dissipation|energy relaxation]]. Since the quantum system is in the ground state, interference with the outside world cannot make it move to a lower state. If the energy of the outside world (that is, the "temperature of the bath") is kept lower than the energy gap between the ground state and the next higher energy state, the system has a proportionally lower probability of going to a higher energy state. Thus the system can stay in a single system eigenstate as long as needed.

Universality results in the adiabatic model are tied to quantum complexity and [[QMA]]-hard problems. The k-local Hamiltonian is QMA-complete for k ≥ 2.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kempe |first1=J. | author1-link = Julia Kempe |last2=Kitaev |first2=A. |author-link2=Alexei Kitaev |last3=Regev |first3=O. |title=The Complexity of the Local Hamiltonian Problem |date=2006-07-27 |journal=SIAM Journal on Computing |issn=1095-7111 |volume=35 |issue=5 |pages=1070–1097 |arxiv=quant-ph/0406180v2 |doi=10.1137/S0097539704445226}}</ref> QMA-hardness results are known for physically realistic [[lattice models]] of [[qubits]] such as<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Biamonte |first1=J. D. |last2=Love |first2=P. J. |date=2008-07-28 |title=Realizable Hamiltonians for Universal Adiabatic Quantum Computers |journal=Physical Review A |volume=78 |issue=1 |article-number=012352 |arxiv=0704.1287 |bibcode=2008PhRvA..78a2352B |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.78.012352 |s2cid=9859204}}</ref>

<math>
H = \sum_{i}h_i Z_i + \sum_{i<j}J^{ij}Z_iZ_j + \sum_{i<j}K^{ij}X_iX_j
</math>

where <math>Z, X</math> represent the [[Pauli matrices]] {{nowrap|<math>\sigma_z, \sigma_x</math>.}} Such models are used for universal adiabatic quantum computation. The Hamiltonians for the QMA-complete problem can also be restricted to act on a two dimensional grid of [[qubits]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Oliveira |first1=R. |last2=Terhal |first2=B. M. |date=2008-11-01 |title=The complexity of quantum spin systems on a two-dimensional square lattice |journal=Quantum Information & Computation |volume=8 |pages=0900–0924 |arxiv=quant-ph/0504050 |bibcode=2005quant.ph..4050O |doi=10.26421/QIC8.10-2 |s2cid=3262293 |number=10}}</ref> or a line of quantum particles with 12 states per particle.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Aharonov |first1=D. |last2=Gottesman |first2=D. |last3=Irani |first3=S. |last4=Kempe |first4=J. | author4-link = Julia Kempe |title=The Power of Quantum Systems on a Line |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |volume=287 |issue=1 |pages=41–65 |date = 2009-04-01 |doi = 10.1007/s00220-008-0710-3 |arxiv = 0705.4077 |bibcode = 2009CMaPh.287...41A|s2cid=1916001 }}</ref> If such models were found to be [[physically realizable]], they too could be used to form the building blocks of a universal adiabatic quantum computer.

In practice, there are problems during a computation. As the Hamiltonian is gradually changed, the interesting parts (quantum behavior as opposed to classical) occur when multiple [[qubit]]s are close to a tipping point. It is exactly at this point when the ground state (one set of qubit orientations) gets very close to a first energy state (a different arrangement of orientations). Adding a slight amount of energy (from the external bath, or as a result of slowly changing the Hamiltonian) could take the system out of the ground state, and ruin the calculation. Trying to perform the calculation more quickly increases the external energy; scaling the number of qubits makes the energy gap at the tipping points smaller.

==Adiabatic quantum computation in satisfiability problems==
Adiabatic quantum computation solves satisfiability problems and other combinatorial search problems, particularly such problems that can be formulated as the ground state of an [[Ising model]] or a [[Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization|QUBO]] problem.

Satisfiability problems seek a state that satisfies
<math>
	C_1 \wedge C_2 \wedge \cdots \wedge C_M
</math>. This expression contains the satisfiability of M clauses, for which clause <math>C_i</math> has the value True or False, and can involve n bits. Each bit is a variable <math>x_j\in \{ 0,1\}</math> such that <math>C_i</math> is a Boolean value function of <math>x_1, x_2, \dots , x_n</math>. QAA solves this kind of problem using quantum adiabatic evolution. It starts with an Initial Hamiltonian <math>H_B</math>:

<math>
	H_B=H_{B_1}+H_{B_2}+\dots+H_{B_M}
</math>

where <math>H_{B_i}</math> shows the Hamiltonian corresponding to the clause <math>C_i</math>. Usually, the choice of <math>H_{B_i}</math> won't depend on different clauses, so only the total number of times each bit is involved in all clauses matters. Next, it goes through an adiabatic evolution, ending in the Problem Hamiltonian <math>H_P</math>:

<math>
	H_P=\sum\limits_{C}^{} H_{P,C}
</math>

where <math>H_{P,C}</math> is the satisfying Hamiltonian of clause C.

It has eigenvalues:

<math>
	h_C(z_{1C},z_{2C}\dots z_{nC})=
	\begin{cases} 
	0 & \mbox{clause } C \mbox{ satisfied} \\ 
	1 & \mbox{clause } C \mbox{ violated}
	\end{cases}
</math>

For a simple path of adiabatic evolution with run time T, consider:

<math>
	H(t)=(1-t/T)H_{B}+(t/T)H_{P}
</math>

and let <math>s=t/T</math>. This results in:

<math>
	\tilde{H}(s)=(1-s)H_{B}+sH_{P}
</math>, which is the adiabatic evolution Hamiltonian of the algorithm.

In accordance with the adiabatic theorem, start from the ground state of Hamiltonian <math>H_B</math> at the beginning, proceed through an adiabatic process, and end in the ground state of problem Hamiltonian <math>H_P</math>.

Then measure the z-component of each of the n spins in the final state. This will produce a string <math>z_1,z_2,\dots,z_n</math> which is highly likely to be the result of the satisfiability problem. The run time T must be sufficiently long to assure correctness of the result. According to the adiabatic theorem, T is about <math>\varepsilon/g_\mathrm{min}^{2}</math>, where
<math>
	g_\mathrm{min}=\min_{0\le s\le 1}(E_1(s)-E_0(s))
</math> is the minimum energy gap between ground state and first excited state.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Farhi |first1=Edward |last2=Goldstone |first2=Jeffrey |last3=Gutmann |first3=Sam |last4=Sipser |first4=Michael |title=Quantum Computation by Adiabatic Evolution |date=2000-01-28 |eprint=quant-ph/0001106 }}</ref>

==Comparison to gate-based quantum computing==
Adiabatic quantum computing is equivalent in power to standard gate-based quantum computing that implements arbitrary unitary operations. However, the mapping challenge on gate-based quantum devices differs substantially from [[Quantum annealing|quantum annealers]] as logical variables are mapped only to single qubits and not to chains.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Zbinden |first1=Stefanie |title=High Performance Computing |chapter=Embedding Algorithms for Quantum Annealers with Chimera and Pegasus Connection Topologies |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=15 June 2020 |volume=12151 |pages=187–206 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-50743-5_10|isbn=978-3-030-50742-8 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==D-Wave quantum processors==
The [[D-Wave One]] is a device made by Canadian company [[D-Wave Systems]], which claims that it uses [[quantum annealing]] to solve optimization problems.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=M. |last2=Amin |first2=M. |date=11 May 2011 |title=Quantum annealing with manufactured spins |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature10012 |journal=Nature |volume=473 |issue=7346 |pages=194–198 |doi=10.1038/nature10012 |pmid=21562559 |bibcode=2011Natur.473..194J |s2cid=205224761 |access-date=12 February 2021 |quote=Some of the authors are employees of D-Wave Systems Inc.|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="quantanneal">{{cite web |last1=Campbell |first1=Macgregor |title=Quantum computer sold to high-profile client |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn20529-quantum-computer-sold-to-high-profile-client/ |website=New Scientist |access-date=12 February 2021 |date=1 June 2011}}</ref> On 25 May 2011, [[Lockheed-Martin]] purchased a D-Wave One for about US$10 million.<ref name="quantanneal" /> In May 2013, [[Google]] purchased a 512 qubit [[D-Wave Two]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Computing: The quantum company |last=Jones |first=Nicola |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=498 |issue=7454 |pages=286–288 |date=2013-06-20 |doi=10.1038/498286a |bibcode = 2013Natur.498..286J |pmid=23783610|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The question of whether the D-Wave processors offer a speedup over a classical processor is still unanswered. Tests performed by researchers at [[Quantum Artificial Intelligence Lab]] ([[NASA]]), [[University of Southern California|USC]], [[ETH Zurich]], and [[Google]] show that as of 2015, there is no evidence of a quantum advantage.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Boixo |first1=S. |last2=Rønnow |first2=T. F. |last3=Isakov |first3=S. V. |last4=Wang |first4=Z. |last5=Wecker |first5=D. |last6=Lidar |first6=D. A. |last7=Martinis |first7=J.
